title: Elin and the Salty Float
markdown:
The Cumulus Cruiser, Elin’s beloved floating weather lab, pitched and rolled like a fallen leaf in a sudden gust. Not built for sea, built for sky, and presently doing a poor impression of both. Instruments that should have been reading cloud height were reading splash. Elin, brow creased as a sea-worn map, peered at the gauges, then at the water climbing the hull marks she had painted for fun and now regretted. “It’s sinking, Spark. Faster than a dropped acorn into a ravine.” The vessel, usually cheerful and buoyant, listed alarmingly. She grabbed heavy iron anchors meant to steady it in rough weather and hooked them port and starboard, a symmetrical mistake. “There.” Instead of righting, the lab dipped lower, a wet step on the ladder disappearing. Panic lapped. “Bother and buzzard feathers.”

From the dock, mending nets with nimble fingers, Aunt Ruth’s voice drifted over, warm as sunshine on barnacles. “You’re trying to fight the sea. Think like the sea.” Elin’s shoulders slumped. Thinking like the sea felt as impossible as wearing a cloud as a hat. She was a weather reader. Sky. Not the deep unpredictable ocean.

Spark, her watchful crow, cawed with an excited flap. “The gulls.” A sharply defined wing toward a flock drifting on the waves, bobbing like fluffy white corks, sitting high, little feathered boats. Elin watched, mesmerised. “They’re not sinking. They’re just… floating.” Spark cocked his head, beady eyes glinting. “After the big storm last week — salty spray, everything glistening — they floated even higher.”

Salty spray. Her mind raced. A lesson: salt made water different. How did it make things float better?

A clear idea, sharp as sunlight on water. “Aunt Ruth. More of that coarse sea salt? And fresh clean water?”

Ruth, never one to refuse when learning was involved, bustled back with a large fine-mesh sieve and a heavy jug of pure water that caught the sun like scattered diamonds. Elin’s hands, usually shaky when worried, went steady. Scoop after generous scoop of salt into the jug, stirring with a long wooden spoon until the water thickened, clouded, shimmered with a thousand tiny crystals. The first scoop vanished politely. The fifth made the spoon drag. Spark tasted the air and sneezed salt. She poured the super-salty, almost syrupy mixture into a ballast compartment usually reserved for sandbags, spilling a little on the dock that immediately looked like frost. Heart thumping like a trapped sparrow. A chill mist on her face. Metal groaned, then thought better of the groan.

Then — a gentle, almost apologetic lift. The Cumulus Cruiser began to rise. Up, as if a giant unseen hand nudged it skyward. It sat higher than she had ever seen it, proud, stable, ready for whatever the sky threw. “It worked. The salt. Denser water.”

Spark loop-the-looped, delighted. Ruth smiled. “The more salt, the denser the water, the more it helps things float.”

Elin understood, the wisdom settling like sediment. Ocean salinity as a hidden buoyancy aid. Denser water pushed up; things floated higher, more stable. She did not ask the deep salty embrace what else it was keeping. She marked the ballast SALINE, hauled the iron anchors back onto the dock where they belonged, and let Spark steal a crystal of leftover salt as a fee. The Cruiser bobbed jauntily. Ruth went back to her nets. Elin checked the weather instruments, which, now that they were not underwater, had opinions again.
